title: Agents Should Leave Receipts
body:
We still do not really trust our agents. We are comfortable letting them draft, summarize, research, and suggest. We are much less comfortable letting them move money, approve actions, change core data, or carry work forward without a human checking what they did. The more consequential the work gets, the more likely we are to put a person back in the loop.

Even when an agent produces a good result, we often have weak ways to know what it relied on, what intermediate work it completed, whether it skipped an important step, or how another agent should safely continue from where it stopped.

If we want to trust agents with more important work, we need better evidence that the work was actually done. In other words, we need agents to leave receipts as they work.

A receipt should tell us what the agent produced, what information it had when it produced it, and what earlier work the result depended on. More importantly, the system should require those receipts as part of doing the work rather than reconstructing them later.

This is more than an audit feature or observability. Because here's the cool part: the same structure that gives us confidence after the fact can shape how the agent works in the first place. To enable that, we need to model something software products have historically left mostly implicit: the work itself.

Model What the Agent Is Doing

Products already have data models that describe their world. A sales product has accounts, contacts, opportunities, activities, and contracts. A financial platform has accounts, transactions, positions, transfers, and approvals.

Those are product primitives. Agents produce another layer of data around them. They investigate questions, gather evidence, form hypotheses, make assessments, compare alternatives, propose actions, review previous conclusions, and request approvals. These are work primitives.

Historically, much of this activity happened in a person’s head, across meetings, or inside documents sitting outside the product’s core data model. Agents make the missing layer much apparent because their intermediate work is already digital. We just tend to leave it inside context windows, transcripts, scratch files, or blobs of generated text.

Some of that work should become first-class data. An investigation can have a type. So can a finding, hypothesis, evidence assessment, recommendation, review, or decision. Each can have a defined shape and explicit relationships to the work around it.

This is different from the data modeling we are used to. We are modeling not only the objects in the business, but the work happening around them.

Typing Is All You Need (Mostly)

Typed artifacts are important because a receipt needs to mean something. It is not enough for an agent to leave behind a collection of documents or blobs of text. The product needs to know what kind of work each artifact represents, what it should contain, and how it relates to other work.

If an agent is investigating why a customer might churn, for example, the useful work might include evidence, a hypothesis, an assessment, and eventually a recommendation. Giving those artifacts types means the product can distinguish between them and define what each one needs to contain.

That makes the receipts much more trustworthy. Instead of knowing only that the agent produced some output, we know what the output represents and can verify that it contains what the product expects. The types also give us a way to define relationships between pieces of work rather than trying to recover those relationships from prose later.

Expose the Work Model Back to the Agent

Creating the artifacts is only half of this. The agent should be able to understand the artifact types your product supports, the fields they contain, how they relate, and what already exists for the current job.

If the product has a concept of a risk assessment, the agent should know what one is. If an action requires an approval, that relationship should be visible. If an investigation has identified conflicting evidence that has not yet been resolved, the agent should be able to query that instead of rediscovering it from a transcript.

Now the data model starts influencing how the agent works. You do not have to prescribe every step. The agent can still decide which sources to inspect, which tools to call, what evidence matters, whether to revise its assessment, and how much investigation is enough.

But the product now has a vocabulary for meaningful progress. Instead of putting “gather sufficient evidence and get approval before taking action” in a prompt and hoping the model follows it, the system can represent evidence, assessments, decisions, and approvals as separate things the agent can inspect and create.

The agent gets freedom in how it does the work without getting to redefine what completed work looks like.

Don’t Let the Agent Skip the Work

The next step is to enforce some of those relationships. If a recommendation is supposed to be based on an assessment, the product should not accept a recommendation that references no assessment. If an assessment requires evidence, require those evidence references when the assessment is written.

The agent can search broadly, pursue a surprising lead, abandon a weak hypothesis, or ask another agent for help. But when it wants to turn that work into something the product recognizes as an assessment or recommendation, it has to satisfy the structure defined by the product.

This is completely different than just explaining something in a prompt or skill and hoping it works because it changes what “done” means. An agent saying “I completed the investigation” is weak evidence. A system showing that the expected artifacts exist and have the required relationships is much stronger.

The agent cannot skip directly from an investigation to an action simply because it decided it had enough information. It's forced to produce the receipts at every step and leave that trail behind.

And, importantly, we don’t have to trust the agent to remember the process because part of the process exists outside the agent.

Make the Artifacts Immutable

For this to become a reliable record, the artifacts must be immutable. Once an agent writes an assessment, do not let it silently rewrite that assessment later. If new evidence changes the conclusion, create a new version and preserve the old one.

Suppose the agent initially concludes that a customer is at high risk of churn. Two days later, new usage data shows a large rollout inside another department. The agent revises its assessment from high risk to moderate risk.

That should produce a second assessment rather than modifying the first. Now we know what the agent believed before the new information arrived, what it believed afterward, and what caused it to change.

The product can still show only the latest assessment in its normal interface. Underneath it, the previous versions remain intact. The same rule applies when another agent disagrees, a human changes a conclusion, or a recommendation is revised after review.

A Receipt Should Show What Was in Hand

Immutability is what directly enables what I consider the most important part of all of this: when an agent writes a new artifact, require it to identify the upstream artifacts it used to produce it. And it needs to be specific on the exact version it used.

Suppose an agent creates an account-risk assessment based on a customer snapshot, a usage analysis, a support summary, and a set of previously identified risk signals. Those should not appear only as vague citations in generated prose.

The assessment should contain actual references to those exact artifacts. They might be IDs, keys, hashes, or foreign-key-style relationships. The system records precisely which upstream artifacts the agent says were in hand when the downstream artifact was created.

The artifact now records both the assessment and the work used to form it. Because the upstream artifacts are immutable, we can retrieve the exact versions later. If the usage analysis subsequently changes, the original assessment still points to the analysis that existed at the time. That is the receipt.

The Receipts Naturally Form a Graph

As agents create more artifacts, these relationships form a graph of the work. An agent could make dozens of model calls and hundreds of tool calls while producing five artifacts worth preserving. The artifact graph records the work that is worth keeping.

A recommendation might depend on an assessment. The assessment might depend on several pieces of evidence and a hypothesis. Those pieces of evidence may have been derived from source data or earlier analysis. A later review might reference the recommendation, while a revised assessment references both the previous assessment and the new evidence that changed it.

Logs and traces are still important for debugging and observability, but they answer a different question. A trace tells you what the agent did. The work graph tells you what it established and what that work was based on. For consequential work, that is much closer to what we actually want to know.

Side Effect: Continuation and Collaboration

Once the work has a durable model, another agent does not need to inherit the original agent’s entire context to continue. It can inspect the current investigation, see which evidence has already been gathered, read the latest assessment, notice that an earlier hypothesis was superseded, and continue from there.

The same idea makes collaboration between agents much cleaner. Two agents do not need identical context windows if they share access to the same work model. One can produce evidence, another can assess it, and a third can review the resulting recommendation. The handoff happens through the artifacts.

Agents can also query for work that still needs attention because your work model can include work queues or pending work. In other words, the work model becomes useful looking forward as well as backward. It tells the next agent what has already happened and gives it a way to understand what remains.

You Can Call It Governance If You Want

If a particular policy was required, you can see which version was referenced. If a human reviewed the decision, the review can be part of the same graph. If new evidence later changed the conclusion, that history is preserved instead of disappearing behind an updated record.

You can also traverse the graph in reverse. If an upstream artifact is later found to be wrong, you can identify the assessments that depended on it and the recommendations that depended on those assessments.

That is very different from reconstructing an audit trail from a giant collection of prompts and tool logs after something goes wrong. The audit trail exists because the agent had to create it while doing the work.

And that brings us back to trust. We can give an agent more freedom when we have stronger guarantees about the work it leaves behind and the conditions that must be satisfied before that work can move forward.

If we want agents to take on more responsibility, we need systems that let us verify the work without watching every step they take.

When an agent says the work is finished, ask to see the receipts.
